newsitem.title: USA: Cancer Society-yearly mammograms for women in 40s.
newsitem.headline: Cancer Society-yearly mammograms for women in 40s.

text.p: The National Cancer Institute said on Monday it may soon have new recommendations for mammography for women aged 40-49.
The institute's statement came one day after the American Cancer Society announced a change in its guidelines.

The cancer society said on Sunday it was urging women in their 40s to have annual mammograms -- an X-ray to detect breast cancer. The society's previous guidelines had urged women in their 40s to have mammograms every year or two.

"The research evidence now tells us that by beginning a program of annual mammography at age 40, women can give themselves the best chance of detecting cancer early, when there is a higher opportunity for long-term survival, and more treatment options," cancer society president Dr. Myles Cunningham said in a statement.

This was at odds with the U.S. government's National Cancer Institute, which stirred controversy in 1993 when it dropped a recommendation for routine mammograms for women aged 40-49. The institute still recommends regular mammograms for older women.

Numerous studies have shown that mammograms for women aged 50-69 could reduce the breast cancer death rate by one-third. But studies on younger women have produced less clear-cut evidence of life-saving benefits.

The controversy continued this year at a so-called consensus conference for the institute on the mammogram issue, which had aimed at clarifying the question but ended up stirring even more controversy by recommending that women in their 40s must decide for themselves.

On Monday, the institute said in a statement that one of its expert panels was "nearing completion of its work to develop clear recommendations to the NCI about screening mammography for women in their 40s."
The National Cancer Advisory Board, the institute's presidentially appointed panel, could reach a decision on new recommendations this week, possibly Thursday, an institute spokesman said.
Mammography has been a useful, though not perfect, tool in the fight against breast cancer, the single leading cause of death for American women in their 40s.

Cancer experts generally agree that women over 50 should get routine mammograms and that most women under 40 do not need them. The debate centers on whether benefits of mammography outweigh risks for women age 40 to 49, when detection of tumors is difficult but early diagnosis can be crucial.

For women with no symptoms of breast cancer, the cancer society recommends monthly breast self-examinations for women over 20, a clinical breast examination every three years for women between 20 and 40, an annual clinical breast examination for women over 40 and a yearly mammogram for women over 40.
The American College of Radiology gave strong backing to the cancer society's new recommendations, and said it has modified its own guidelines to urge more frequent screening for women in their 40s.

The radiologists said in a statement that recent Swedish research gave "unquestionable proof" that annual mammograms can reduce cancer deaths among women age 40-49 by at least 25 percent and possibly as must as 45 percent.

In related news, scientists at a cancer society conference outside Washington said a form of a gene, known as the CYP17 gene, may contribute to breast cancer. The gene is involved in production of estrogen, a hormone linked to breast cancer.

That form, or allele, of the gene was more common in women who began to menstruate at a younger age. This may help explain why those women are believed to be at higher risk for breast cancer and further research could also help identify women who entered menarche later but may also still be at high risk for breast cancer.

Scientists have identified two genes, BRCA1 and BRCA2, linked to breast and ovarian cancer. But these genes only explain about five percent of all cases of breast cancer. Scientists are still searching for other genetic and environmental explanations for breast cancer.
